claims.text: The material is a FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate.
The baseline coating is processed entirely in an inert atmosphere without post-deposition oxidizing annealing.
The intervention is post-deposition annealing in an atmosphere containing 2–5% O2 in inert gas.
Oxidizing post-deposition annealing will selectively oxidize and enrich copper at the FeNiCrCoCu coating surface.
Chromium will oxidize to a lesser extent than copper during the annealing treatment.
The annealing treatment will form a thin, adherent, copper-enriched mixed oxide layer consisting primarily of Cu2O/CuO with possible chromium oxides.
At high temperature, copper and minor chromium segregate and oxidize at the wear surface.
The copper-enriched mixed oxide behaves as a self-lubricating, refractory tribofilm.
The oxide tribofilm decreases friction and mitigates abrasive and adhesive wear.
Relative to the inert-processed baseline, oxidizing-annealed coatings will have lower friction coefficients during high-temperature cyclic sliding.
Relative to the inert-processed baseline, oxidizing-annealed coatings will have lower high-temperature wear rates.
The annealed coating will exhibit a copper-rich oxide surface film detectable by XPS or Auger spectroscopy.
The proposed mechanism applies to cyclic sliding at 400–600 °C and contact loads typical of service.
The effect may differ outside the stated thermal and mechanical boundaries.
Excessive oxidation may make the oxide layer brittle and cause spallation under cyclic loads.
Failure to form a distinct copper-enriched oxide layer would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both friction and wear relative to the inert baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
